title: Missed a Credit Card Payment? What to Do Next
description: Missed a credit card payment? What to do in the first 48 hours, when it hits your credit report, how to ask for the late fee back and how to prevent it.

cover.alt: An alarm clock next to a blank card and a yellow sticky note

keywords: missed credit card payment what happens if you miss a credit card payment late fee waiver late payment credit report
takeaways: Pay at least the minimum as soon as you notice. Card issuers usually report only after 30 days late.
Call and ask for the late fee to be waived. A first miss often gets a yes.
Set up autopay for the minimum so it cannot happen again.
body:
You open your banking app, glance at your credit card, and your stomach drops. The payment was due three days ago, and you never sent it. Maybe you forgot. Maybe payday landed late. Either way, it is missed, and you are wondering how much damage is done.

Take a breath. A missed credit card payment is one of the more fixable money mistakes, as long as you handle it in the right order. What happens next depends far less on the miss itself and far more on how long you wait. This guide walks through the timeline in three parts: the first 24 hours, the days before day 30, and what to do if you are already past that point. It also gives you the exact words to use to ask for the late fee back, plus the five minute fix that stops this happening again.

## Two clocks start ticking the day you miss

Most people treat a missed payment as one problem. It is actually two, running on different clocks.

The first clock is the fee clock, and it starts right away. Your card company can charge a late fee as soon as your payment is late by even a day. Under the federal safe harbor amounts that apply in the US, that fee can be up to $30 for a first late payment, and up to $41 if you are late again within the next six billing cycles. The fee can never be more than the minimum payment you owed. You may have seen headlines about an $8 cap on late fees. That rule was struck down in court in April 2025, so the higher amounts still stand.

The second clock is the credit report clock, and it runs much slower. Card companies generally do not report a payment as late to the credit bureaus until it is at least 30 days past due. Pay inside that window and the miss never appears on your report at all. That gap between the two clocks is your opportunity, because a reported late payment can stay on your report for up to seven years.

One more cost runs in the background: interest. If you carry a balance, it keeps adding up while the payment is missing, and paying late can cost you your grace period on new purchases too.

## The first 24 hours: pay something today

Do not wait until you can pay the whole balance. The most useful thing you can do today is send at least the minimum payment, right now, through the issuer's own app or website, which is usually the fastest way to get it credited.

Two details are worth knowing. First, a payment counts as on time if the company receives it by 5 p.m. on the due date, in the time zone shown on your statement. You are past that point now, but it explains why paying the issuer directly beats mailing a check or using a bill pay service that takes days to deliver the money. Second, save the payment confirmation. A screenshot takes five seconds and settles any argument later about when you paid.

Once the payment is in, check three things: whether a late fee has been added, how much you still owe, and when the next payment is due. Catching up on this month does not always cover next month, and if your next statement is already out, its due date is still coming.

## Before day 30: call and ask for the fee back

Here is the step many people skip, because asking feels awkward. Call the number on the back of your card and ask for the late fee to be removed. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the US consumer finance regulator, openly suggests doing exactly this. Issuers waive fees as a courtesy all the time, especially for a first miss on an otherwise clean record.

Pay first, then call. It is a much easier conversation when the money is already on its way.

### Say it like this

"Hi, my name is [your name]. I am calling about my card ending in [last four digits]. My payment was due on [date], and I missed it. I have already made the payment today, so the account is up to date. I can see a late fee of $[amount] on my account. I have had this card for [length of time], and this is the first payment I have ever missed on it. Would you be able to remove the late fee as a one time courtesy?"

Then stop talking and let them answer. If the answer is no, stay friendly and ask one follow up: "Is there anything you can do at all, even a partial credit?" If they still say no, thank them and note the date and the name of the person you spoke to. A second call a few days later sometimes gets a different answer.

While you have them on the phone, ask two more questions. Will this be reported to the credit bureaus? If you paid within 30 days of the due date, the answer should be no. And does it change your interest rate? Not on money you already owe, for reasons covered below.

| Timing                | What usually happens                                                              | On your credit report?                     |
|-----------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------|
| Day 1                 | A late fee of up to $30 can be added to your account                             | No                                         |
| Days 2 to 29          | Interest keeps running on your balance                                            | No, if you pay before day 30               |
| Day 30                | The miss can now be reported as 30 days late                                      | Yes, and it can stay for up to seven years |
| Day 60 and beyond     | A penalty APR can be applied to your existing balance, after 45 days of warning   | Yes, as 60 days late                       |
| Around day 120 to 180 | The company may close the account and charge off the balance, which you still owe | Yes, a serious mark                        |

## If you are already past 30 days

Maybe you are reading this a month or more after the due date. The plan changes a little, but it does not disappear.

Pay as much as you can today, even if it is not the full amount. Every week matters. A payment reported as 30 days late is a problem, and one that rolls into 60 or 90 days late is a bigger one. Payment history is the biggest single part of a FICO credit score, at 35 percent, so stopping the slide now is worth real money later.

Once you have paid, ask about a goodwill adjustment, where the company agrees to take the late mark off your report as a gesture, even though the payment really happened. They are not required to do it, and many will say no. Your chances are best if the miss was a one off, your record is otherwise clean, and the account is now up to date. Put the request in writing, short and honest.

Then check your credit reports to see exactly what has been recorded. Mistakes do happen. If a report shows a late payment for a month you actually paid on time, dispute it with the bureau and send your payment confirmation as proof. If the balance has grown past what you can catch up on monthly, it may be time for a fuller payoff plan instead. Read next: [How to Pay Off Credit Card Debt Fast](/blog/pay-off-credit-card-debt-fast/). And if you are rebuilding after a rough patch, the basics still work, one on time payment at a time. Read next: [How to Build Credit From Scratch](/blog/how-to-build-credit-from-scratch/).

## Penalty APR: the quiet cost of reaching 60 days late

You may see the words penalty APR in your card agreement. APR is just the yearly interest rate on your card. A penalty APR is a higher rate the company switches you to when you pay late, often close to 30 percent.

Federal rules limit the damage in one useful way. A penalty APR can only be applied to money you already owe once you are more than 60 days late, and the company has to warn you 45 days ahead. It can apply to new purchases sooner, depending on your agreement, which is one more reason to stop using the card until you are caught up. There is a way back, too. After six minimum payments in a row on time, the company must lower the rate on your older balance back to what it was.

Here is that rate jump in real money. This example is an illustration with made up numbers, not a quote from any card. Say you owe $1,000. At a 24 percent APR, interest runs at about $20 a month. At a penalty APR of 29.99 percent, it is about $25 a month. That is roughly $60 a year extra, paid for owing the same $1,000. Staying under 60 days late keeps you away from this cost entirely.

## If you cannot pay the minimum at all

Sometimes the problem is not forgetting. It is that the money is not there. If that is you, still call the card company, ideally before the next due date. Many issuers run hardship programs that can lower your payment, pause fees, or cut your rate for a set period. Asking early gives you the most options.

Be honest about the order of bills, too. Rent, utilities, and food come before a credit card. A late card payment is fixable. Losing your home is a different scale of problem. If several cards are in the same position, free help exists through nonprofit credit counselling agencies. Longer term, a small emergency cushion is what usually stops this repeating, even if you build it slowly. Read next: [How to Build an Emergency Fund on a Low Income](/blog/emergency-fund-on-a-small-income/).

## Finish with autopay, so this is the last time

You have paid, you have called, the fee is sorted. Spend five more minutes and make it a one off.

Set up autopay in the app or on the website. You link your bank account and pick an amount. You usually get three choices:

- Minimum payment only. This protects your credit report and avoids late fees, but interest keeps building on the balance left over. A safety net, not a plan.
- Full statement balance. No interest and no thinking required, but the amount changes monthly, so you need a cushion in your bank account to avoid an overdraft.
- A fixed amount above the minimum that you know you can afford every month. Steady and predictable.

Pick a payment date a few days before the due date, not on the day itself, so a slow transfer never makes you late. Turn on due date alerts as a back up, and keep a small buffer in the account autopay pulls from. Read next: [Monthly Money Review: A 20-Minute Checklist](/blog/monthly-money-review/).

One last option, if the due date itself is the problem. Most issuers will let you move it to a few days after payday, with one short call or a few taps in the app.

## Frequently asked questions

### I missed my payment by one day. Will it hurt my credit score?

Almost certainly not. Issuers generally do not report a payment as late until it is at least 30 days past due, so a payment made a day or a week late stays off your report. You may still be charged a late fee, which is worth a phone call.

### How much is a late fee on a credit card?

In the US, up to $30 for a first late payment, and up to $41 if you are late again within the next six billing cycles. It cannot be more than the minimum payment that was due. Your exact fee is in your card agreement.

### Can a late payment really stay on my credit report for seven years?

Yes, it can stay on your report for up to seven years. It does the most harm early on, though, and matters less as time passes, especially if every payment after it is on time.

### My autopay failed. What should I do?

Pay manually right away, because the late fee lands on your account first either way. Then call and explain what happened. If the failure was on the issuer's side, that is a strong case for a refund of the fee and any interest it caused. If your bank account was short, lower autopay to the minimum and move the date to just after payday.

One missed payment feels awful, but it is a short problem with a long tail only if you ignore it. Pay today, make the call, set up autopay, and this stays a story about a fee, not a seven year mark on your credit report.

## A quick note

This article is general information about how credit card payments and late fees work, based mostly on US rules, which differ in the UK, Canada, and Australia. It is not personal financial advice. Check your own card agreement for your terms, and consider talking to a nonprofit credit counselling service or a qualified adviser about your situation.
